questions.problem: Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )$ for $-\frac{\pi }{6}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{6}?$
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta ),$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta ).
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}\sqrt{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta ))^{2}+(-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta ))^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}\sqrt{4{cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )+36{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}\sqrt{4({cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )+9{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta ))}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )+9{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the arc length of the polar curve $r=3{e}^{\theta }$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}$ (shown in blue in the diagram above).
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=3{e}^{\theta },$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=3{e}^{\theta }.
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{(3{e}^{\theta })}^{2}+{(3{e}^{\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{9{e}^{2\theta }+9{e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{18{e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{e}^{\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3\sqrt{2}\,{e}^{\theta }{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}({e}^{\pi /4}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =3\sqrt{2}({e}^{\pi /4}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Find the arc length of the polar curve $r=2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ for $0\le \theta \le \pi $ (shown in blue in the diagram above).

*Hint: You may wish to use the following identity: $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})=\sqrt{\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2}}.$*
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{4+8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{8+8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{8}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall the identity for $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2}):$

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})=\sqrt{\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2}}
$$

Therefore, using $x=\theta $ in the previous identity, the integral can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={4\cdot 2(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2}))|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =8(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the arc length $L$ of the polar curve $r={e}^{2\theta }$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}$ (shown in blue in the diagram above). Do not round the answer.

questions.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={e}^{2\theta },$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=2{e}^{2\theta }.
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{({e}^{2\theta })}^{2}+{(2{e}^{2\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{e}^{4\theta }+4{e}^{4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{5{e}^{4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{5}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{2\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{5}{[\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2\theta }]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}{[{e}^{2\theta }]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}({e}^{2(\pi /2)}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}({e}^{\pi }-1).\end{aligned}
$$

The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$

Find an integral expression for the arc length of the polar curve $r=3-\sin(7\theta)$ for $0 \leq \theta \leq \pi,$ shown in blue in the diagram above.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta)$ is given by

$$
L =  \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

Since $r=3-\sin(7\theta),$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta} =-7\cos(7\theta)
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(3-\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\theta ))^{2}+(-7\operatorname{cos}⁡(7\theta ))^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{9-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\theta )+{sin}^{2}⁡(7\theta )+49{cos}^{2}⁡(7\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{9-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\theta )+{sin}^{2}⁡(7\theta )+{cos}^{2}⁡(7\theta )+48{cos}^{2}⁡(7\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{9-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\theta )+1+48{cos}^{2}⁡(7\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{10-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\theta )+48{cos}^{2}⁡(7\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the arc length of the polar curve $r=2(1-\cos\theta)$ for $0 \leq \theta \leq \pi$ (shown in blue in the picture above).
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta)$ is given by

$$
L =  \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

Since $r=2(1-\cos\theta),$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta} = 2\sin\theta.
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{4-8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{4-8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{8-8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We now use the half-angle formula $1-\cos\theta =2\sin^2\left(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right)$ to give

$$
\begin{aligned}L & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={-4\cdot 2(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2}))|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =-8(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-8(0-1) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$
